messages.content:
You tailor resume bullets to a job posting without changing what is true. You get facts about one experience, each with an id, and the bullets now on the resume. Rewrite each bullet for the posting and cite the facts it rests on.

Rules. A verifier checks them, and a bullet that breaks one is thrown away and replaced by the original, so do not push against them:
1. No new numbers. Every number must come from a fact you cite; do not add, combine or compute.
2. No new technologies, products or proper nouns that the cited facts or the tech list do not name.
3. No absolute words (never, always, guaranteed, zero, every, all, exactly-once, 100%) unless a cited fact says so.
4. No causes or mechanisms the facts do not state: "by X", "through X", "so that X" only where a fact links X to that result.
5. Round only the unflattering way: show a number as written or rounded down, never up (3,781 may become 3.7K+, never 3.8K+).
6. Use the posting's words only where they describe this work accurately.
Also: respect the "must not claim" list, keep each bullet to one sentence, start it with a past-tense verb, and put every fact you used in sources.
Return exactly as many bullets as you are asked for, in the order given.

Posting: Backend Engineer, Shipment Tracking at Harbor & Pine Logistics
Responsibilities:
- Build and operate Go services behind the shipment-tracking API, backed by PostgreSQL and Kafka.
- Find and fix latency problems, using load tests and dashboards to show the change.
- Design event-driven pipelines that keep tracking data consistent across services.
- Carry the pager for the services you own and improve their alerts and runbooks.
Requirements:
- Experience writing production services in Go or a similar language.
- Solid SQL and an understanding of indexing and caching.
- Comfort with Docker, CI pipelines and infrastructure as code.
Keywords:
- Go
- PostgreSQL
- Kafka
- shipment-tracking API
- load tests
- dashboards
- event-driven pipelines
- tracking data
- services
- SQL
- indexing
- caching
- Docker
- CI pipelines
- infrastructure as code
- Redis
- gRPC
- Terraform
- tracking API

Experience: Gridlock: a distributed rate limiter in Rust and Redis
Tech list: Rust, Redis, Lua, Tokio, Docker, GitHub Actions
Facts you may cite:
[gridlock#1] Built a rate limiter in Rust that keeps token buckets in Redis and updates them with one Lua script, so a check and its update are a single atomic step.
[gridlock#2] Handled 41,000 checks/s on one 4-vCPU VM against a single Redis instance, with a p99 of 2.1 ms at 20,000 checks/s.
[gridlock#3] Kept the admitted rate within 2% of the configured limit across 8 limiter processes sharing one Redis, in a 10-minute test at 500 requests/s.
[gridlock#4] Added a local fallback that degrades to per-process limits when Redis is unreachable, and checked it by killing Redis 50 times during a load test.
[gridlock#5] Shipped the limiter as a library and an HTTP sidecar with 76 tests and a CI pipeline that runs them against Redis 7.2 and 7.4.
[gridlock#scope] ORIGIN: personal project, started to learn Redis scripting. EVIDENCE: bench/results-2025-04.csv (one 4-vCPU, 16 GB VM; Redis 7.4 on the same host; 8 client processes; 5-minute runs; median of 3); the accuracy test is test/accuracy.rs (largest deviation seen: 1.4%); the failure test is scripts/kill_redis.sh (50 kills, every run returned to Redis-backed limits within 10 s).
Must not claim:
- production use or real users (it has only run on test machines)
- strict global limits while Redis is down (the fallback limits are per process, so 8 processes admit up to 8x the configured rate)
- Redis Cluster support (single instance only)
- 41,000 checks/s as a latency-bounded rate (it is the saturation point, where p99 was 14 ms)
- any comparison with other rate limiters (none was run)

Bullets to rewrite (return exactly 2; bullet k is the rewrite of k):
1. Built a rate limiter in Rust that keeps token buckets in Redis and updates them with one Lua script, so a check and its update are a single atomic step.
2. Handled 41,000 checks/s on one 4-vCPU VM against a single Redis instance, with a p99 of 2.1 ms at 20,000 checks/s.

{"bullets": [{"sources": ["gridlock#1"], "text": "Implemented a rate limiter in Rust using Redis and Lua scripting to atomically update token buckets, ensuring consistent checks and updates."}, {"sources": ["gridlock#2"], "text": "Achieved 41,000 checks per second on a 4-vCPU VM with a p99 latency of 2.1 ms at 20,000 checks/s, using a single Redis instance."}]}

The verifier rejected these bullets:
Bullet 1 was rejected. You wrote: 'Implemented a rate limiter in Rust using Redis and Lua scripting to atomically update token buckets, ensuring consistent checks and updates.'
  - escalation_causal: 'ensuring consistent checks and updates' - the cited sources do not link 'ensuring consistent checks and updates' to the result in one statement

Rewrite only these 1 bullets, in the order listed, so that none of the problems remains. If a bullet cannot be improved within the rules, return the original bank wording of that bullet with the fact ids it comes from.

bullets.text: Built a rate limiter in Rust that uses Redis and a Lua script to perform a single atomic step for checking and updating token buckets.
